new_statements.quote: The Malwi stress pattern is in such a way that the stress falls oneither on the strongest syllable or the heaviest available foot as shown in the following words: /‵naː.ɡəɳ/ ‘snake’(‵SH) /‵ʋaːn.d̪ə.roː/ ‘monkey’(‵SLH) [...] In Malwi, when the weight of two or more syllables is the same, the stress falls on the syllable which Has the most ‘high’ vowel as the nucleus. [...] /iː/ > /uː/ > /oː/ >/eː/ >/aː/ [...] In case, if two syllables are of the same weight and have the same vowel as their nucleus, then the stress will fall on the penultimate syllable, as in the word /‵ɡoː.loː/ ‘circle’.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive, Hindi-type system: syllable weight is moraic (short vowel 1 mora, long vowel 2, each coda consonant 1; light/heavy/superheavy, max 3 moras, p.93-94). Primary stress goes to the heaviest syllable of the word (e.g. 'na:.gəɳ SH-initial, hʊ.'kho: L'H, ba:.'lo:ɽ H'S, dʒə.'mi:n.d̪a:r L'SS). When two or more syllables tie in weight, Malwi (unlike Hindi's rightmost-nonfinal rule) stresses the syllable whose vowel is higher (i: > u: > o: > e: > a:, e.g. ha:.'d̪i:, ra:.kʰo:.'ɽi: HH'H, but 'pe:.la: 'HH); if the tied syllables also share the same vowel, the penult is stressed ('go:.lo:). Bhattacharya 1975 (Appendix 1, pp.271-273, Central Malvi of Indore-Ujjain-Dewas) independently gives quality/closure-driven rules for isolated words: monosyllables tonic; in disyllables the syllable with /a/ is tonic and a schwa syllable is never stressed, otherwise the first syllable is stressed, except that two closed syllables with the same vowel (sək'kər) or two /a/ syllables with an open first (da'lan) take final stress; trisyllables and compounds apply the same rules to their parts.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described in Upadhyay 2019 (only primary stress marked). Bhattacharya 1975 speaks only of 'primary word-stress'; no secondary stress rules given.
new_statements.exceptions: Upadhyay 2019: obligatory schwa deletion in the weak (rightmost) syllable of a foot in connected speech resyllabifies the word, shortens the preceding long vowel and 'might cause stress shift from one syllable to another' (pp.96-100); a final heavy syllable is extrametrical in the Hindi rules she cites but Malwi ties are resolved by vowel height instead. Bhattacharya 1975: rules hold for words 'uttered isolated'; 'This stress pattern is modified, when a word is used in a sentence, depending on the intonation used therein'; words over three syllables are compounds whose latter member carries the pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress in citation forms (Upadhyay: 'everything is restricted to the domain of the word', p.100; Bhattacharya: isolated words, sentence intonation may override). Both descriptions are of the Ujjaini/Central Malvi variety (Ujjain district; Indore-Ujjain-Dewas). Note the two accounts differ in mechanism (moraic weight + vowel height vs. vowel quality /a/-attracting, schwa-repelling + syllable closure) but agree that stress is not fixed and is computed from syllable content.
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand stress descriptions are of the prestige Ujjaini / 'Central Malvi' variety (Ujjain, Indore, Dewas districts, Madhya Pradesh): Upadhyay 2019 recorded 30 speakers in Ujjain district; Bhattacharya 1975 analysed stress only for Central Malvi (CM) among her four dialects (CM, Rajwadi, Sondhwadi, Umathwadi). Upadhyay spells the language 'Malwi' (= Malvi, mup, malv1243; not the Malwai dialect of Punjabi). Baskaran 2011 (silent on stress) describes Malvi as spoken in Rajasthan. Upadhyaya 1960's only accent remark (final-syllable emphasis on a-final words) concerns Nimadi, a separate Glottolog language (nima1243), not Malvi.
